AES.analogy: A bank vault where the same key locks and unlocks the door — fast, sturdy, and only as safe as whoever holds that one key.

contrast.headline: Symmetric bulk data encryption
contrast.edge: AES is the cipher itself; the others are modes or protocols that use it.

RSA.analogy: A mailbox with a public slot anyone can drop letters into, but only the owner's private key opens the back door.

contrast.headline: Asymmetric encryption and signatures
contrast.edge: RSA handles key exchange and signing; TLS is the protocol built around it.

ECC.analogy: A tiny padlock forged from much harder steel — a 256-bit ECC key guards as well as a 3072-bit RSA brick.

contrast.headline: Small-key asymmetric cryptography
contrast.edge: ECC gets RSA-level strength from much smaller keys, ideal for mobile and IoT.

PKI.analogy: The whole passport system — the issuing office, the photo ID, the border check, and the list of stolen passports.

contrast.headline: Certificate trust framework
contrast.edge: PKI is the entire trust system; CA, CRL and OCSP are its parts.

CA.analogy: The passport office: you trust a stranger's ID only because a government you trust stamped it.

contrast.headline: Issues and signs certificates
contrast.edge: The CA is the trusted signer; the rest are formats and status checks.

CRL.analogy: A bouncer's printed list of banned IDs — reliable, but only as current as the last time it was printed.

contrast.headline: Published list of revoked certs
contrast.edge: A CRL is a periodic downloadable list; OCSP answers per certificate in real time.

OCSP.analogy: Phoning the bank at checkout to ask whether this one card is still valid, instead of reading last week's list.

contrast.headline: Real-time certificate status check
contrast.edge: OCSP checks one certificate live; a CRL is a bulk list downloaded periodically.

SHA.analogy: A fingerprint scanner for data — change a single comma and the fingerprint comes out completely different.

contrast.headline: One-way hash for integrity
contrast.edge: SHA proves data unchanged, but without a key it cannot prove who sent it.

HMAC.analogy: A wax seal pressed with a stamp only you and the recipient own — it proves the letter is untouched and came from you.

contrast.headline: Keyed hash for authenticity
contrast.edge: HMAC adds a shared secret to a hash, giving integrity plus authenticity.

GCM.analogy: A tamper-evident envelope that both hides the letter and shows if anyone opened it.

contrast.headline: Authenticated AES encryption mode
contrast.edge: GCM encrypts and authenticates in one pass, unlike plain counter mode.

CTM.analogy: A numbered ticket roll: each ticket number is encrypted into a one-time pad and XORed with your data.

contrast.headline: Turns block cipher into stream
contrast.edge: Counter mode encrypts but does not authenticate; GCM adds the authentication.

PEM.analogy: A shipping envelope with a clear 'BEGIN CERTIFICATE' label — the box format, not the contents' security.

contrast.headline: Base64 certificate file format
contrast.edge: PEM is only a text encoding format; it provides no security on its own.

GCMP.analogy: Swapping a good padlock on the Wi-Fi door for a modern one that also flags tampering.

contrast.headline: WPA3 Wi-Fi encryption protocol
contrast.edge: GCMP is GCM applied to Wi-Fi frames in WPA3, replacing WPA2's CCMP.

ECB.analogy: Translating a book word by word with a fixed dictionary — every repeated word looks identical, so patterns shine through.

contrast.headline: Insecure basic block mode
contrast.edge: ECB encrypts identical blocks identically, leaking patterns; never use it for data.

CBC.analogy: A daisy chain where each link is twisted by the one before it, so identical links never look the same.

contrast.headline: Chained block encryption mode
contrast.edge: CBC hides patterns that ECB leaks, but needs a random IV and is sequential.

CFB.analogy: A cipher used like a dripping tap: it feeds back its own output to encrypt a stream bit by bit.

contrast.headline: Self-synchronizing stream mode
contrast.edge: CFB turns a block cipher into a stream cipher that recovers from lost bits.

IV.analogy: Shuffling the deck before every game, so the same hand never deals out the same way twice.

contrast.headline: Randomizes each encryption
contrast.edge: An IV is not secret, but it must never repeat with the same key.

TPM.analogy: A tiny safe welded onto the motherboard that holds keys and remembers exactly how the computer booted.

contrast.headline: On-board key and boot integrity
contrast.edge: A TPM is built into one device; an HSM is a dedicated enterprise appliance.

GPG.analogy: The free, open-source edition of the same sealed-envelope service PGP sells.

contrast.headline: Open-source PGP implementation
contrast.edge: GPG implements the OpenPGP standard freely; PGP was the original product.

PGP.analogy: Sealing a letter with the recipient's padlock and signing it with your personal wax stamp.

contrast.headline: Email encryption and signing
contrast.edge: PGP uses a web of trust between users instead of central certificate authorities.

IKE.analogy: Two diplomats meeting first to agree on a secret language before any real messages are sent.

contrast.headline: Negotiates IPSec security associations
contrast.edge: IKE only negotiates keys and SAs; IPSec then protects the actual traffic.

DSA.analogy: A notary stamp: it proves who signed a document but never hides what the document says.

contrast.headline: Digital signatures only
contrast.edge: DSA only signs; unlike RSA it cannot be used to encrypt data.

PFS.analogy: Burning each day's codebook at sunset, so a key stolen tomorrow can't unlock yesterday's mail.

contrast.headline: Unique key per session
contrast.edge: PFS uses ephemeral keys, so stealing the server key can't decrypt past sessions.

CER.analogy: Tuning a biometric door until it wrongly lets in strangers exactly as often as it wrongly locks out staff.

contrast.headline: Biometric accuracy balance point
contrast.edge: CER is where FAR equals FRR; a lower CER means a more accurate system.

EER.analogy: The same balance point as CER, just under its other name, like 'soda' and 'pop'.

contrast.headline: Alias for crossover rate
contrast.edge: EER and CER are the same thing: where false accepts equal false rejects.

HSM.analogy: An armored bank vault for keys — the keys are used inside it and never leave.

contrast.headline: Dedicated tamper-resistant key hardware
contrast.edge: An HSM is a dedicated, tamper-resistant appliance, unlike a TPM built into one device.

TLS.analogy: A sealed pneumatic tube between your browser and the server: anyone can see the tube, nobody can read the capsule.

contrast.headline: Encrypts data in transit
contrast.edge: TLS is the protocol; AES, RSA and PKI are the building blocks inside it.

HTTPS.analogy: Ordinary web mail, but sent in a locked armored truck instead of on a postcard.

contrast.headline: Web traffic over TLS
contrast.edge: HTTPS is just HTTP wrapped in TLS on port 443.

SSH.analogy: A private, soundproof phone line to a remote server's command prompt.

contrast.headline: Encrypted remote shell access
contrast.edge: SSH is the secure tunnel on port 22; SCP and SFTP move files through it.

SMTP.analogy: The postal trucks moving letters between post offices — by default the letters are postcards anyone can read.

contrast.headline: Server-to-server email delivery
contrast.edge: Plain SMTP on port 25 is cleartext; SMTPS or STARTTLS adds encryption.

RDP.analogy: Sitting at a computer across the world through a window — great for admins, a magnet for attackers if left open.

contrast.headline: Graphical remote desktop access
contrast.edge: RDP on 3389 should never face the internet; put it behind a VPN or gateway.

VPN.analogy: A private underground tunnel running beneath a crowded public road.

contrast.headline: Encrypted tunnel over untrusted networks
contrast.edge: A VPN is the tunnel concept; IPSec and TLS are protocols that build it.

IPSec.analogy: Armoring every individual package at the shipping dock, no matter which app packed it.

contrast.headline: Network-layer encryption suite
contrast.edge: IPSec secures every IP packet at Layer 3, unlike TLS which secures one application.

IDS.analogy: A security camera with an alarm — it sees the burglar and shouts, but doesn't lock the door.

contrast.headline: Detects and alerts only
contrast.edge: An IDS is passive and only alerts; an IPS sits inline and blocks.

IPS.analogy: A security guard standing in the doorway who physically stops anyone suspicious.

contrast.headline: Inline detection and blocking
contrast.edge: An IPS sits inline and blocks traffic; a false positive can block legitimate users.

WAF.analogy: A bouncer who reads every web request word by word and turns away the ones carrying SQL or script tricks.

contrast.headline: Layer 7 web app filtering
contrast.edge: A WAF understands HTTP itself, unlike a network firewall that sees only IPs and ports.

VLAN.analogy: Painting colored lanes on one shared floor so each department's traffic stays in its own lane.

contrast.headline: Logical Layer 2 segmentation
contrast.edge: A VLAN splits one physical switch into isolated broadcast domains.

LAN.analogy: The hallways inside one building — everyone nearby, connected without leaving the premises.

contrast.headline: Single-site local network
contrast.edge: A LAN covers one site; MAN covers a city and WAN spans regions.

WAN.analogy: The highway system connecting cities — the internet is the biggest highway network of all.

contrast.headline: Long-distance network links
contrast.edge: A WAN links distant sites, usually over carrier or internet connections.

WLAN.analogy: The same office hallways, but you walk them through the air instead of along cables.

contrast.headline: Wi-Fi local network
contrast.edge: A WLAN is a LAN over 802.11 radio, so it needs WPA2 or WPA3 protection.

MAN.analogy: A city's subway system — bigger than one building, smaller than the national railway.

contrast.headline: City-wide network
contrast.edge: A MAN sits between LAN and WAN, covering a campus or city.

PAN.analogy: The invisible bubble around you where your phone, earbuds and watch talk to each other.

contrast.headline: Personal short-range network
contrast.edge: A PAN covers a few meters around one person, typically Bluetooth or NFC.

FW.analogy: A border checkpoint that checks every vehicle's papers against a rulebook before letting it through.

contrast.headline: Rule-based traffic filtering
contrast.edge: A basic firewall filters by IP, port and protocol; an NGFW also understands applications.

DNSSEC.analogy: A notarized phone book, where every entry carries a signature proving nobody forged the number.

contrast.headline: Signed, authenticated DNS records
contrast.edge: DNSSEC proves DNS answers are authentic but does not encrypt them.

mnemonic.phrase: Domain Names Signed Securely Each Certificate

DDNS.analogy: A phone book that updates itself whenever you move to a new apartment.

contrast.headline: Auto-updated DNS records
contrast.edge: DDNS keeps a name pointing at an IP that changes, often after DHCP renewals.

DHCP.analogy: A hotel front desk handing every arriving guest a room number, a map, and a checkout time.

contrast.headline: Automatic IP address assignment
contrast.edge: DHCP hands out IP settings; a rogue DHCP server can redirect a whole network.

PAC.analogy: A small note taped inside the browser telling it which side door to use for each address.

contrast.headline: Browser proxy routing script
contrast.edge: A PAC file only picks a proxy per URL; it encrypts nothing itself.

WEP.analogy: A screen door on a bank vault — it looks like a lock, but anyone can push through in minutes.

contrast.headline: Broken original Wi-Fi encryption
contrast.edge: WEP's reused IVs make it crackable in minutes; never deploy it.

WPA.analogy: A quick patch on WEP's broken lock while the proper door was still being built.

contrast.headline: Interim TKIP Wi-Fi fix
contrast.edge: WPA used TKIP as a stopgap; WPA2 brought proper AES encryption.

WPA2.analogy: A solid deadbolt for Wi-Fi — strong, unless the shared password is weak enough to guess.

contrast.headline: AES-CCMP Wi-Fi security
contrast.edge: WPA2-Personal falls to offline password guessing; WPA3's SAE fixes that.

WPS.analogy: A spare key hidden under the doormat with only an eight-digit lock on the box.

contrast.headline: Convenient but brute-forceable pairing
contrast.edge: WPS PINs are checked in two halves, so brute force takes only hours; disable it.

TCP.analogy: Registered mail: numbered, signed for, and resent if it gets lost.

contrast.headline: Reliable connection-oriented transport
contrast.edge: TCP guarantees ordered delivery through a 3-way handshake; UDP skips all that.

UDP.analogy: Shouting announcements across a stadium — fast, but nobody confirms they heard you.

contrast.headline: Fast connectionless transport
contrast.edge: UDP has no handshake or retransmission, ideal for DNS, VoIP and streaming.

DNS.analogy: The internet's phone book, turning names you remember into numbers machines dial.

contrast.headline: Translates names to IPs
contrast.edge: Plain DNS is unauthenticated, which is why poisoning works and DNSSEC exists.

SCP.analogy: Handing a box through the secure SSH tunnel instead of throwing it over the fence.

contrast.headline: File copy over SSH
contrast.edge: SCP copies files over SSH but, unlike SFTP, cannot browse or resume.

RAS.analogy: The old dial-up back door into the office network, from before VPNs became standard.

contrast.headline: Legacy remote network access
contrast.edge: RAS is the legacy dial-in concept; VPNs replaced it with encrypted internet tunnels.

TTLS.analogy: Building a secure tunnel to the gatekeeper first, then whispering your password inside it.

contrast.headline: Tunneled EAP authentication method
contrast.edge: EAP-TTLS needs only a server certificate, unlike EAP-TLS which needs client certificates too.

PPTP.analogy: A tunnel built from cardboard: still standing, but it collapses the moment anyone pushes.

contrast.headline: Obsolete insecure VPN protocol
contrast.edge: PPTP's MS-CHAPv2 authentication is broken; replace it with IPSec or TLS VPNs.

NetBIOS.analogy: Shouting names down an old office corridor to find colleagues — chatty and easy to eavesdrop on.

contrast.headline: Legacy Windows name service
contrast.edge: NetBIOS leaks host and share information; disable it where not needed.

mnemonic.phrase: Network eavesdroppers Track Broadcasts In Old Systems

RPC.analogy: Calling a coworker and asking them to run a task on their desk as if it were yours.

contrast.headline: Executes procedures on remote hosts
contrast.edge: RPC lets programs call code remotely, a frequent lateral movement path.

API.analogy: A restaurant menu and waiter: you order through the counter, never walking into the kitchen.

contrast.headline: Programmatic interface between systems
contrast.edge: An API exposes functions to other programs, so it needs authentication and rate limits.

ICMP.analogy: The network's radar ping and error notes — 'are you there?' and 'can't get there from here'.

contrast.headline: Diagnostics and error messages
contrast.edge: ICMP powers ping and traceroute but can be abused for floods and reconnaissance.

NAT.analogy: A company switchboard: outsiders see one main number, never the extensions behind it.

contrast.headline: Maps private IPs to public
contrast.edge: NAT conserves IPv4 addresses and hides internal hosts, but it is not a firewall.

PAT.analogy: One apartment building address, with each resident's mail sorted by apartment number.

contrast.headline: Many hosts, one IP
contrast.edge: PAT tracks sessions by port number so many hosts share one public IP.

SFTP.analogy: A full file-cabinet service delivered through the SSH tunnel — browse, upload, rename, resume.

contrast.headline: Full file transfer over SSH
contrast.edge: SFTP is an SSH subsystem on port 22, unrelated to FTP despite the name.

FTP.analogy: Mailing your files and your password on postcards for every mail carrier to read.

contrast.headline: Cleartext file transfer
contrast.edge: FTP on 20/21 sends credentials in cleartext; replace it with SFTP or FTPS.

FTPS.analogy: The same old FTP postcards, now sealed in TLS envelopes.

contrast.headline: FTP secured with TLS
contrast.edge: FTPS is FTP over TLS with separate data channels; SFTP is a different, SSH-based protocol.

BGP.analogy: The internet's postal agreements between countries — whoever announces a route is mostly trusted.

contrast.headline: Routes between autonomous systems
contrast.edge: BGP trusts route announcements, so hijacks can reroute whole networks' traffic.

L2TP.analogy: An empty armored-truck chassis: it carries cargo, but you must add IPSec for the armor.

contrast.headline: Tunneling without built-in encryption
contrast.edge: L2TP only tunnels; security comes entirely from pairing it with IPSec.

SMTPS.analogy: The same mail trucks between post offices, now with the cargo locked in TLS boxes.

contrast.headline: Email delivery over TLS
contrast.edge: SMTPS encrypts mail between hops, typically implicit TLS on port 465.

NTP.analogy: The town clock everyone sets their watch by — if it's wrong, logs and Kerberos tickets break.

contrast.headline: Synchronizes device clocks
contrast.edge: Accurate time keeps logs correlatable and Kerberos working within its five-minute skew.

SNMP.analogy: A building manager's clipboard checking every thermostat and meter remotely — old versions leave the clipboard on the lobby counter.

contrast.headline: Network device monitoring
contrast.edge: SNMPv1 and v2c use cleartext community strings; SNMPv3 adds authentication and encryption.

NNTP.analogy: The courier service for old internet bulletin boards called Usenet newsgroups.

contrast.headline: Usenet article transfer
contrast.edge: NNTP on port 119 carries Usenet articles; it is largely legacy today.

TFTP.analogy: A loading dock with no ID check, used to drop boot files onto devices quickly.

contrast.headline: Unauthenticated lightweight file transfer
contrast.edge: TFTP has no authentication at all; keep it on isolated management networks.

RDS.analogy: A hotel of remote desktops, where many users check into their own sessions on one server.

contrast.headline: Microsoft multi-user remote desktops
contrast.edge: RDS is the Windows service hosting sessions; RDP is the protocol carrying them.

SOAP.analogy: Sending a formal letter in a strict XML envelope with every field filled out.

contrast.headline: XML web service messaging
contrast.edge: SOAP is a rigid XML standard with built-in WS-Security, unlike lightweight REST.

SVC.analogy: Calling a taxi when you need a ride, instead of keeping a private driver on salary.

contrast.headline: On-demand temporary WAN circuit
contrast.edge: An SVC is built per session; a PVC stays permanently provisioned.

DCS.analogy: The control room of a refinery, coordinating thousands of valves and sensors across the plant.

contrast.headline: Plant-wide process control
contrast.edge: A DCS controls one plant locally; SCADA supervises assets spread over wide areas.

MIB.analogy: The catalog of every gauge and dial a managed device exposes to SNMP.

contrast.headline: SNMP object database
contrast.edge: The MIB defines what can be read; OIDs address individual entries.

NMS.analogy: The building manager's central dashboard watching every device's vital signs.

contrast.headline: Central network monitoring console
contrast.edge: The NMS is the manager; SNMP agents on devices answer its queries.

SIP.analogy: The receptionist who dials, connects, and hangs up calls but never carries the conversation itself.

contrast.headline: Sets up VoIP sessions
contrast.edge: SIP only signals calls; the voice itself travels separately, usually over RTP.

OID.analogy: A Dewey Decimal number pointing to exactly one book in the SNMP library.

contrast.headline: Unique SNMP object address
contrast.edge: An OID is just an address; the MIB defines what lives there.

SPD.analogy: The customs rulebook deciding which packages get sealed, waved through, or rejected.

contrast.headline: IPSec traffic policy rules
contrast.edge: The SPD decides what to protect; IKE negotiates how to protect it.

EAP.analogy: A universal ID checkpoint that accepts passports, badges or fingerprints — whichever method you plug in.

contrast.headline: Pluggable authentication framework
contrast.edge: EAP is a framework, not a method; EAP-TLS and EAP-TTLS are methods inside it.

DKIM.analogy: A tamper-evident wax seal on outgoing mail, verifiable with a public stamp published in DNS.

contrast.headline: Signs email for authenticity
contrast.edge: DKIM signs the message itself; SPF only checks which server sent it.

SPF.analogy: A guest list published by your domain naming which mail servers may send on its behalf.

contrast.headline: Authorized sending servers list
contrast.edge: SPF validates the sending server's IP; it says nothing about message tampering.

DMARC.analogy: The rulebook telling mail servers what to do with a letter that fails the seal and guest-list checks.

contrast.headline: Enforcement policy for SPF/DKIM
contrast.edge: DMARC tells receivers to quarantine or reject failures and sends reports back.

DMAC.analogy: The apartment number on an envelope inside the building — it only matters on the local hallway.

contrast.headline: Destination Layer 2 address
contrast.edge: A destination MAC only gets a frame across one local hop, then gets rewritten.

AH.analogy: A tamper seal on a transparent envelope — proves nothing changed, but anyone can read it.

contrast.headline: IPSec integrity without encryption
contrast.edge: AH authenticates packets but does not encrypt, and it breaks through NAT.

ESP.analogy: A sealed, opaque, tamper-evident envelope for every packet.

contrast.headline: IPSec encryption and integrity
contrast.edge: ESP encrypts and authenticates, which is why it is used far more than AH.

CRS.analogy: A ready-made blacklist of known tricks that a WAF bouncer memorizes before the shift.

contrast.headline: OWASP default WAF rules
contrast.edge: CRS is the rule set; the WAF is the engine that enforces it.

SWG.analogy: A customs office for outbound traffic, checking where employees browse and what they download.

contrast.headline: Filters outbound web traffic
contrast.edge: A SWG protects users going out; a WAF protects apps coming in.

APT.analogy: A burglar who moves into your attic for months, quietly learning the house before stealing anything.

contrast.headline: Long-term stealthy targeted intrusion
contrast.edge: APTs are patient, resourced and targeted, often nation-state backed.

DDoS.analogy: Hiring a thousand people to stand in a shop doorway so real customers can't get in.

contrast.headline: Distributed availability attack
contrast.edge: DDoS attacks availability from many sources at once, unlike a single-source DoS.

MITM.analogy: A mail carrier who opens, reads, and reseals every letter before delivering it.

contrast.headline: Intercepts traffic between parties
contrast.edge: MITM breaks confidentiality and integrity; TLS with proper certificate validation defeats it.

XSS.analogy: Slipping a fake instruction card into a restaurant's menu so every diner who reads it follows your orders.

contrast.headline: Injects scripts into pages
contrast.edge: XSS runs in the victim's browser; SQLi runs against the server's database.

SQLi.analogy: Writing 'and also open the safe' on a bank withdrawal slip, and the teller just does it.

contrast.headline: Injects commands into queries
contrast.edge: Parameterized queries stop SQLi at the source; a WAF only adds a filter layer.

CVE.analogy: A public wanted-poster ID number, so everyone talks about the same vulnerability by the same name.

contrast.headline: Unique vulnerability identifier
contrast.edge: A CVE names a vulnerability; CVSS tells you how severe it is.

CVSS.analogy: A hurricane scale for vulnerabilities — a single number from 0 to 10 that says how bad the storm is.

contrast.headline: 0–10 severity score
contrast.edge: CVSS rates technical severity; real priority also depends on your environment.

C2.analogy: The puppeteer's strings: infected machines quietly phone home to receive their next orders.

contrast.headline: Attacker's remote control channel
contrast.edge: Blocking or detecting C2 beacons cuts attackers off from compromised hosts.

IoC.analogy: Muddy footprints and a broken window latch — clues proving someone already got in.

contrast.headline: Forensic evidence of breach
contrast.edge: IoCs are reactive artifacts like hashes and IPs; TTPs describe attacker behavior.

RAT.analogy: A trojan horse with a remote-controlled puppet inside, letting the attacker drive your PC from afar.

contrast.headline: Malware for covert remote control
contrast.edge: A RAT disguises itself as legitimate software, then hands full control to its operator.

TTPs.analogy: A burglar's signature style — how they case houses, pick locks, and escape — rather than one fingerprint.

contrast.headline: Attacker behavior patterns
contrast.edge: TTPs, mapped in MITRE ATT&CK, are harder for attackers to change than IoCs.

PUP.analogy: The extra toolbars that sneak in when you click 'Next, Next, Finish' too quickly.

contrast.headline: Unwanted bundled software
contrast.edge: PUPs install with technical consent, so they're unwanted rather than strictly malicious.

SEH.analogy: The emergency exit plan of a Windows program — attackers rewrite the map so the exit leads to their code.

contrast.headline: Windows exception handling chain
contrast.edge: SEH overwrites hijack the exception handler; SafeSEH and SEHOP mitigate them.

MFA.analogy: A vault needing a key, a code, and your fingerprint — stealing one isn't enough.

contrast.headline: Two or more factor types
contrast.edge: MFA needs different factor types; two passwords are still single-factor.

SSO.analogy: A wristband at a festival: show ID once at the gate, then walk into every stage.

contrast.headline: One login, many apps
contrast.edge: SSO is convenient but makes one login a high-value target; pair it with MFA.

SAML.analogy: A signed letter of introduction from your employer that a partner company accepts at its door.

contrast.headline: XML federated authentication
contrast.edge: SAML passes signed XML assertions, typical for enterprise web SSO.

OAuth.analogy: Handing a valet key to the parking attendant — it drives the car but can't open the trunk.

contrast.headline: Delegated authorization tokens
contrast.edge: OAuth grants scoped access to resources; it is authorization, not authentication.

OIDC.analogy: The valet key from OAuth plus a name badge proving who is holding it.

contrast.headline: Identity layer over OAuth
contrast.edge: OIDC adds an ID token so OAuth can also authenticate the user.

LDAP.analogy: Asking the company switchboard operator to look up anyone's office, phone and team.

contrast.headline: Directory query protocol
contrast.edge: LDAP on 389 is cleartext; LDAPS on 636 adds TLS.

RADIUS.analogy: A central security desk that every Wi-Fi access point and VPN calls to check IDs.

contrast.headline: Centralized AAA for network access
contrast.edge: RADIUS uses UDP and encrypts only the password; TACACS+ encrypts everything.

mnemonic.phrase: Remote Authentication Desk In Use Somewhere

RBAC.analogy: Keycards issued by job title: every nurse gets the nurse card, every doctor the doctor card.

contrast.headline: Permissions through job roles
contrast.edge: RBAC ties permissions to roles, not people, which simplifies onboarding and audits.

IAM.analogy: The HR and security office deciding who you are, what badge you get, and when it's revoked.

contrast.headline: Identity lifecycle and access
contrast.edge: IAM covers all identities; PAM focuses only on high-privilege accounts.

PAM.analogy: Checking out the master key from a guarded cabinet, on camera, for a limited time.

contrast.headline: Controls privileged accounts
contrast.edge: PAM vaults, rotates and records admin credentials instead of leaving them standing.

TOTP.analogy: A secret handshake that changes every 30 seconds, known only to your phone and the server.

contrast.headline: Time-based one-time codes
contrast.edge: TOTP codes come from a shared seed plus the current time, so clocks must agree.

TACACS+.analogy: The network gear's private security desk, checking ID, permissions and logs in three separate steps.

contrast.headline: Cisco AAA for device admin
contrast.edge: TACACS+ uses TCP 49, encrypts the full payload, and separates all three A's.

mnemonic.phrase: Terminal Admins Can Authenticate Commands Securely

KDC.analogy: The ticket office at a theme park: prove who you are once, then collect tickets for each ride.

contrast.headline: Kerberos ticket-issuing server
contrast.edge: The KDC contains both the AS and TGS, usually on a domain controller.

Kerberos.analogy: A theme park wristband system: verify at the gate once, then trade the wristband for ride tickets.

contrast.headline: Ticket-based network authentication
contrast.edge: Kerberos never sends passwords over the network and rejects tickets with excessive clock skew.

mnemonic.phrase: Keys expire rapidly, but every request obtains service

TACACS.analogy: The same Cisco security desk as TACACS+, the version the exam really means today.

contrast.headline: Cisco device AAA protocol
contrast.edge: Modern TACACS+ encrypts the whole payload, unlike RADIUS which hides only the password.

mnemonic.phrase: Total Admin Command Access Control Security

TGT.analogy: The theme-park wristband: it doesn't open rides itself, but it lets you collect ride tickets.

contrast.headline: Proof of login in Kerberos
contrast.edge: A stolen TGT enables pass-the-ticket attacks, so its lifetime is kept short.

TGS.analogy: The ride-ticket booth where you show your wristband to get a ticket for one specific ride.

contrast.headline: Issues Kerberos service tickets
contrast.edge: The TGS exchanges a TGT for a service ticket; the AS issues the TGT.

AS.analogy: The park entrance gate that checks your ID and puts on your wristband.

contrast.headline: Kerberos login verification
contrast.edge: The AS verifies the user once; later requests go to the TGS.

ST.analogy: A single ride ticket that only works on the one attraction printed on it.

contrast.headline: Access to one service
contrast.edge: A service ticket is accepted by one service, encrypted with that service's key.

SAE.analogy: Two people proving they know the same password without ever saying it aloud, so eavesdroppers learn nothing.

contrast.headline: WPA3 password-based key exchange
contrast.edge: SAE (Dragonfly) resists offline dictionary attacks that break WPA2-PSK.

ABAC.analogy: A door that opens only if your department, clearance, location and the time of day all match the policy.

contrast.headline: Policy over many attributes
contrast.edge: ABAC evaluates many attributes per request, far more granular than roles alone.

UAC.analogy: Windows tapping your shoulder: 'Are you sure you want to use admin powers for this?'

contrast.headline: Windows elevation prompt
contrast.edge: UAC runs users with standard rights and asks before elevating any action.

RuBAC.analogy: A sign on the door saying 'closed after 6 PM' that applies to everyone, whoever they are.

contrast.headline: System-wide rules, not identity
contrast.edge: RuBAC applies the same rules to everyone, such as firewall ACLs or time windows.

AAA.analogy: A nightclub: check your ID, decide which rooms you can enter, and log what you ordered.

contrast.headline: Authenticate, authorize, account
contrast.edge: AAA is the framework; RADIUS and TACACS+ are protocols that carry it out.

ACL.analogy: A doorman's clipboard checked top to bottom — the first matching line decides who gets in.

contrast.headline: Ordered permit and deny rules
contrast.edge: ACLs are processed in order with an implicit deny at the end.

FRR.analogy: A fingerprint door so fussy it keeps locking out the very employees it should admit.

contrast.headline: Legitimate users wrongly rejected
contrast.edge: FRR is an inconvenience error; FAR is the security error of admitting impostors.

NGFW.analogy: A border guard who not only checks passports but opens luggage and knows which app you're carrying.

contrast.headline: Application-aware firewall
contrast.edge: An NGFW identifies applications and users, not just ports, using deep packet inspection.

DPI.analogy: A customs officer who opens every parcel and reads the contents, not just the shipping label.

contrast.headline: Inspects full packet payloads
contrast.edge: DPI reads payloads, but encrypted traffic must be decrypted first to inspect it.

DMZ.analogy: The lobby of a secured building: visitors can reach reception, but not the offices upstairs.

contrast.headline: Buffer zone for public servers
contrast.edge: Public-facing servers live in the DMZ so a breach doesn't reach the internal LAN.

DLP.analogy: Security at the exit scanning everyone's bags for documents they shouldn't be carrying out.

contrast.headline: Stops sensitive data leaving
contrast.edge: DLP classifies and blocks sensitive data in motion, at rest, and in use.

NAC.analogy: A health screening at the door: no badge, missing patches, or no antivirus means no entry.

contrast.headline: Admission based on device posture
contrast.edge: NAC checks device identity and health before granting any network access.

ZTNA.analogy: A building where every single door checks your badge, even after you're already inside.

contrast.headline: Per-request access, never implicit trust
contrast.edge: ZTNA grants access per application, replacing a VPN's broad network-level trust.

MDM.analogy: A remote control for the company's phones: push settings, enforce PINs, wipe a lost device.

contrast.headline: Central mobile device control
contrast.edge: MDM enforces policy on devices, including remote wipe if one is lost.

SCADA.analogy: Mission control for a power grid, watching and steering equipment spread across hundreds of miles.

contrast.headline: Supervises dispersed industrial systems
contrast.edge: SCADA supervises widely spread assets, often over legacy and insecure protocols.

ICS.analogy: The nervous system of factories and utilities, where a hack can move physical machinery.

contrast.headline: Controls physical industrial processes
contrast.edge: In ICS, availability and safety come first, so patching is slow and careful.

PLC.analogy: A rugged little brain bolted to a machine, running its on-off logic all day in the factory heat.

contrast.headline: Ruggedized machine controller
contrast.edge: PLCs directly drive machinery; Stuxnet showed what happens when they are reprogrammed.

RTU.analogy: A remote weather station reporting gauge readings back to mission control.

contrast.headline: Field data collector for SCADA
contrast.edge: RTUs sit at remote sites and relay telemetry over long distances.

RFID.analogy: A name tag that announces itself to any reader nearby, whether you meant it to or not.

contrast.headline: Radio tags for badges, tracking
contrast.edge: RFID badges can be skimmed and cloned at a distance; shielded sleeves help.

UTM.analogy: A Swiss Army knife appliance: firewall, IPS, antivirus and filtering in one box.

contrast.headline: All-in-one security appliance
contrast.edge: A UTM simplifies small networks but creates a single point of failure.

UPS.analogy: A battery bridge that keeps the lights on long enough for the generator to start.

contrast.headline: Short-term battery power backup
contrast.edge: A UPS covers minutes of outage; generators handle longer ones.

SED.analogy: A diary that scrambles every word the instant you write it and unscrambles only for the right key.

contrast.headline: Hardware full-disk encryption
contrast.edge: An SED encrypts in the drive's own hardware, independent of the operating system.

UEFI.analogy: A bouncer at the computer's front door who checks the OS's signature before letting it boot.

contrast.headline: Modern firmware with Secure Boot
contrast.edge: UEFI Secure Boot blocks unsigned bootloaders, stopping many rootkits and bootkits.

ESG.analogy: A mailroom inspector who opens every envelope, tosses scams and malware, and stops secrets going out.

contrast.headline: Filters inbound and outbound email
contrast.edge: An ESG is the enforcement point where SPF, DKIM and DMARC checks happen.

PSU.analogy: The heart of a single computer, turning wall current into the steady pulse components need.

contrast.headline: Converts AC to DC
contrast.edge: A PSU powers one device; redundant PSUs remove a single point of failure.

PDU.analogy: A smart power strip for a whole server rack, often with per-outlet monitoring and control.

contrast.headline: Distributes rack power
contrast.edge: A PDU distributes power; it provides no backup unless fed by a UPS.

RAID0.analogy: Splitting a book's pages between two couriers — twice as fast, but lose one courier and the book is gone.

contrast.headline: Striping, speed, no redundancy
contrast.edge: RAID 0 offers zero fault tolerance; one failed drive destroys all data.

RAID1.analogy: Writing every page in two identical notebooks — if one is lost, the other is complete.

contrast.headline: Mirroring two drives
contrast.edge: RAID 1 survives one drive failure but halves usable capacity.

RAID5.analogy: Three friends each hold part of a puzzle plus a checksum, so any one can rebuild a missing piece.

contrast.headline: Striping with single parity
contrast.edge: RAID 5 needs 3+ drives and survives exactly one failure.

RAID6.analogy: The puzzle-sharing friends keep two checksums, so even losing two of them doesn't sink the puzzle.

contrast.headline: Striping with double parity
contrast.edge: RAID 6 needs 4+ drives and survives two simultaneous drive failures.

RAID10.analogy: Two pairs of twin notebooks with the pages split between pairs — fast and fault tolerant.

contrast.headline: Striped mirrors for speed
contrast.edge: RAID 10 needs 4+ drives and gives speed plus redundancy at 50% capacity.

HOT.analogy: A fully furnished, stocked spare office with the lights already on — move in within minutes.

contrast.headline: Immediate failover site
contrast.edge: A hot site meets the shortest RTO but is the most expensive option.

WARM.analogy: A spare office with desks and phones installed, but you still need to bring the files.

contrast.headline: Partially ready backup site
contrast.edge: A warm site balances cost and recovery time, typically hours to days.

COLD.analogy: An empty rented warehouse with power and network jacks, waiting for you to furnish it.

contrast.headline: Empty facility, slow activation
contrast.edge: A cold site is cheapest but takes days or weeks to activate.

RTOS.analogy: A conductor who must hit every beat exactly on time — late is as bad as wrong.

contrast.headline: Deterministic time-critical OS
contrast.edge: An RTOS guarantees response deadlines, so heavy security tooling can be hard to add.

ASLR.analogy: Rearranging a building's room numbers every morning so a burglar's floor plan is always wrong.

contrast.headline: Randomizes memory addresses
contrast.edge: ASLR makes memory-corruption exploits unreliable by hiding where code and data live.

SCAP.analogy: A robotic auditor reading a standard checklist and scanning every machine against it automatically.

contrast.headline: Automated compliance and vuln checks
contrast.edge: SCAP standardizes formats like CVE and CVSS so scanners share the same language.

SDN.analogy: An air-traffic tower directing every plane centrally, instead of each pilot choosing routes alone.

contrast.headline: Centralized software network control
contrast.edge: SDN separates the control plane from switches, so the controller must be well protected.

SD-WAN.analogy: A smart GPS for company traffic, picking the best internet or MPLS link for each app in real time.

contrast.headline: Software-managed WAN links
contrast.edge: SD-WAN optimizes and steers WAN traffic; it is not a security stack alone.

FWaaS.analogy: Renting a firewall in the cloud like a streaming subscription instead of buying a box for every office.

contrast.headline: Cloud-delivered firewall
contrast.edge: FWaaS protects remote users and branches without on-site firewall hardware.

PaaS.analogy: Renting a fully equipped kitchen: you bring the recipe, they maintain the ovens.

contrast.headline: Managed platform for apps
contrast.edge: In PaaS you own your code and data; the provider runs OS and runtime.

SASE.analogy: Moving the whole security checkpoint into the cloud so it follows every user wherever they work.

contrast.headline: Converged cloud network security
contrast.edge: SASE bundles networking and security as one cloud service near the user.

BCP.analogy: The plan for keeping the restaurant serving customers when the kitchen floods.

contrast.headline: Keeps the business operating
contrast.edge: BCP keeps the whole business running; DRP focuses on restoring IT.

DRP.analogy: The step-by-step guide for rebuilding the kitchen after the flood.

contrast.headline: Restores IT after disaster
contrast.edge: A DRP restores technology; the BCP keeps business functions alive meanwhile.

RPO.analogy: How far back the last save point is — lose power now, and you redo everything since then.

contrast.headline: Maximum tolerable data loss
contrast.edge: RPO is measured backward in data lost; RTO is measured forward in downtime.

RTO.analogy: The stopwatch that starts when the lights go out and must not run past the deadline.

contrast.headline: Maximum tolerable downtime
contrast.edge: RTO is how fast you must recover; RPO is how much data you can lose.

GRC.analogy: The steering wheel, the risk map, and the rulebook — making security serve the business and the law.

contrast.headline: Governance, risk and compliance
contrast.edge: GRC aligns security decisions with business goals and regulatory obligations.

SDLM.analogy: The blueprint process for building a house, from sketches to inspection to move-in.

contrast.headline: Structured software build process
contrast.edge: The SDLC methodology structures development; SDLS embeds security into it.

SDLS.analogy: Having the building inspector check every stage of construction, not just the finished house.

contrast.headline: Security in every SDLC phase
contrast.edge: Fixing flaws during design costs far less than patching them after release.

RAD.analogy: Building a quick cardboard model, showing the client, and reshaping it again the same week.

contrast.headline: Fast prototyping development model
contrast.edge: RAD favors speed and prototypes, so security reviews must keep pace with iterations.

PII.analogy: Anything that could point a stranger straight to your front door — name, SSN, face, address.

contrast.headline: Data identifying a person
contrast.edge: PII is any identifying data; PHI is the health-related subset.

PHI.analogy: Your medical chart — anything linking your name to your diagnosis or treatment.

contrast.headline: Health data tied to people
contrast.edge: PHI is health data linked to an identity and regulated under HIPAA in the US.

GDPR.analogy: Europe's privacy rulebook that follows EU residents' data wherever in the world it travels.

contrast.headline: EU personal data regulation
contrast.edge: GDPR applies to any organization processing EU residents' data, with heavy fines.

HIPAA.analogy: The US rulebook that keeps your doctor's files locked and tells clinics how to share them.

contrast.headline: US health data privacy law
contrast.edge: HIPAA governs US healthcare providers, insurers and their business associates.

NIST.analogy: The national cookbook of security recipes that much of the industry follows.

contrast.headline: US cybersecurity standards body
contrast.edge: NIST publishes the CSF and SP 800 series; it is a US federal agency.

SOW.analogy: A contractor's job sheet listing exactly what gets built, by when, and what done looks like.

contrast.headline: Scope of a specific project
contrast.edge: An SOW details one project under the broader terms of an MSA.

COOP.analogy: The government's plan to keep essential services running even if headquarters is unusable.

contrast.headline: Essential functions during crisis
contrast.edge: COOP is the government term for continuity planning of essential functions.

MTTF.analogy: The average lifespan of a light bulb you'll throw away, not fix, when it dies.

contrast.headline: Lifespan of non-repairable items
contrast.edge: MTTF applies to items replaced, not repaired, after failing.

MTTR.analogy: The average time the mechanic needs to get your car back on the road.

contrast.headline: Average time to restore
contrast.edge: Lower MTTR means faster recovery and helps meet the RTO.

MTBF.analogy: How many miles your car usually drives between trips to the repair shop.

contrast.headline: Average uptime between failures
contrast.edge: Higher MTBF means more reliable repairable systems.

MOU.analogy: A handshake on paper: both sides agree on intentions, but no court will enforce it.

contrast.headline: Non-binding statement of intent
contrast.edge: An MOU signals cooperation without legal obligations, unlike an SLA or BPA.

ARO.analogy: How many times a year you expect the basement to flood.

contrast.headline: Yearly incident frequency
contrast.edge: ARO is a frequency, e.g. 0.5 for once every two years.

ALE.analogy: The yearly flood budget: what one flood costs multiplied by how often floods happen.

contrast.headline: Expected yearly loss
contrast.edge: ALE = SLE × ARO; spending more than ALE on a control rarely makes sense.

SLE.analogy: The repair bill from one single basement flood.

contrast.headline: Cost of one incident
contrast.edge: SLE = AV × EF, the loss from one occurrence.

AV.analogy: The price tag on what's at risk before anything bad happens.

contrast.headline: Monetary worth of asset
contrast.edge: AV is the starting point of quantitative risk math: SLE = AV × EF.

BPA.analogy: The formal partnership contract spelling out who invests, who decides, and how profits split.

contrast.headline: Binding partnership terms
contrast.edge: A BPA defines the partnership itself, including roles, profits and responsibilities.

MSA.analogy: The umbrella contract signed once, so each new project needs only a short SOW.

contrast.headline: Umbrella terms for future work
contrast.edge: An MSA sets general terms once; SOWs then define each project.

TOCTOU.analogy: Checking a concert ticket at the gate, then someone swaps it before the scanner reads it.

contrast.headline: Race between check and use
contrast.edge: TOCTOU exploits the gap after a check; atomic operations and locking close it.

mnemonic.phrase: Time Of Check Then Others Use

SLA.analogy: A pizza promise: delivered in 30 minutes or there's a penalty.

contrast.headline: Contracted service performance levels
contrast.edge: An SLA defines measurable uptime and response targets with penalties if missed.

BIA.analogy: Asking each department: if your systems vanished today, what would it cost and how fast must they return?

contrast.headline: Measures disruption impact
contrast.edge: The BIA identifies critical functions and sets RTO and RPO for continuity plans.

ISO.analogy: The international recipe book, with ISO 27001 being the certifiable recipe for an ISMS.

contrast.headline: International standards body
contrast.edge: ISO 27001 can be certified; ISO 27002 provides the control guidance.

EF.analogy: How much of the house a single fire actually burns — 30% of it, say.

contrast.headline: Percentage lost per incident
contrast.edge: EF is a percentage of asset value lost in one incident.

GLBA.analogy: The rulebook telling US banks and lenders to keep your financial details under lock.

contrast.headline: US financial privacy law
contrast.edge: GLBA applies to US financial institutions and requires a written security program.

EULA.analogy: The long legal fine print you scroll past and accept before installing an app.

contrast.headline: Software license terms
contrast.edge: A EULA is the vendor's contract with users; an AUP is the employer's policy.

AUP.analogy: The house rules every employee signs: what you may and may not do with company tech.

contrast.headline: Rules for using systems
contrast.edge: An AUP sets user behavior expectations and supports disciplinary action.

SIEM.analogy: A detective's evidence board pinning together clues from every camera, door log and alarm in the building.

contrast.headline: Centralized log correlation
contrast.edge: A SIEM collects and correlates; it detects but does not respond on its own.

SOC.analogy: The 24/7 security control room where analysts watch the screens and respond to alarms.

contrast.headline: Team monitoring threats 24/7
contrast.edge: The SOC is people and process; SIEM and SOAR are their tools.

SOAR.analogy: A robot assistant that runs the SOC's playbooks automatically the moment an alarm fires.

contrast.headline: Automated response playbooks
contrast.edge: SOAR acts on alerts with automated playbooks; a SIEM only detects them.

EDR.analogy: A flight recorder and bodyguard on every laptop, recording behavior and isolating the machine if needed.

contrast.headline: Endpoint behavior detection, response
contrast.edge: EDR watches behavior on hosts and can isolate them, unlike signature-only antivirus.

XDR.analogy: EDR's bodyguards linked by radio with guards at the email gateway, network and cloud.

contrast.headline: Correlated multi-domain detection
contrast.edge: XDR correlates endpoint, network, email and cloud telemetry in one vendor platform.

IR.analogy: The fire department's drill: detect the smoke, contain the fire, put it out, then learn why it started.

contrast.headline: Structured breach handling
contrast.edge: IR phases: preparation, detection, analysis, containment, eradication, recovery, lessons learned.

UEBA.analogy: A guard who knows everyone's routine and notices when the accountant logs in at 3 AM from abroad.

contrast.headline: Baselines and flags anomalies
contrast.edge: UEBA learns normal behavior and flags deviations, catching insiders and stolen accounts.

AIS.analogy: A neighborhood watch group text, where organizations instantly share descriptions of new burglars.

contrast.headline: CISA automated indicator sharing
contrast.edge: AIS is CISA's free program, built on STIX and TAXII.

TAXII.analogy: The delivery truck carrying threat-intel packages between organizations over HTTPS.

contrast.headline: Transport for threat intel
contrast.edge: TAXII moves the intel; STIX is the language the intel is written in.

STIX.analogy: A common language for describing attackers, so every organization's intel reads the same way.

contrast.headline: Threat intel description format
contrast.edge: STIX describes threat intelligence; TAXII is how it is shared.

NVD.analogy: The library catalog that takes each CVE ID and adds severity scores, product lists and fix notes.

contrast.headline: NIST-enriched CVE database
contrast.edge: CVE names the flaw; the NVD adds CVSS scores and affected product details.

VM.analogy: An apartment inside a building: a full home that shares the building's foundation and plumbing.

contrast.headline: Software-emulated computer
contrast.edge: VMs share a hypervisor, so VM escape is the key isolation risk.

VDI.analogy: Your desk lives in the data center; your laptop is just a window onto it.

contrast.headline: Centrally hosted desktops
contrast.edge: VDI keeps data in the data center, so a lost laptop leaks nothing.

IaaS.analogy: Renting empty land with utilities hooked up — you build and maintain everything on it.

contrast.headline: Rented compute, storage, network
contrast.edge: In IaaS you patch the OS and apps; the provider secures the hardware.

SaaS.analogy: Eating at a restaurant: you just order, the kitchen and dishes are someone else's problem.

contrast.headline: Subscription software via browser
contrast.edge: In SaaS you still own your data, user access and configuration.

CASB.analogy: A chaperone standing between employees and cloud apps, enforcing company rules on what's shared.

contrast.headline: Policy broker for cloud apps
contrast.edge: A CASB brings visibility and DLP to cloud apps, including unsanctioned shadow IT.

MSSP.analogy: Hiring a professional security company to guard your building instead of training your own guards.

contrast.headline: Outsourced security operations
contrast.edge: An MSSP delivers SOC-style monitoring as a service; accountability still stays with you.

L7.analogy: The front desk you actually talk to — web pages, email, and DNS lookups live here.

contrast.headline: User-facing application protocols
contrast.edge: Layer 7 is where WAFs, proxies and most attacks against apps operate.

L6.analogy: The translator and envelope-sealer, handling encoding, compression and encryption.

contrast.headline: Formatting, encryption, encoding
contrast.edge: Layer 6 converts data formats; TLS is commonly mapped here for the exam.

L5.analogy: The meeting organizer who opens, keeps alive, and closes the conversation between apps.

contrast.headline: Manages application sessions
contrast.edge: Layer 5 manages sessions; it is where session hijacking concepts live.

L4.analogy: The shipping department choosing registered mail (TCP) or quick postcards (UDP) and labeling the door number.

contrast.headline: End-to-end delivery and ports
contrast.edge: Layer 4 adds ports and reliability; stateful firewalls track it.

L3.analogy: The postal routing system, reading IP addresses to move packets between cities.

contrast.headline: IP routing and addressing
contrast.edge: Layer 3 routes between networks; routers and IP addresses live here.

L2.analogy: The hallway mail carrier in one building, delivering by MAC address door to door.

contrast.headline: MAC addressing and switching
contrast.edge: Layer 2 moves frames locally; ARP spoofing and VLAN hopping attack here.

L1.analogy: The roads themselves — copper, fiber and radio waves carrying raw bits.

contrast.headline: Cables, signals, radio
contrast.edge: Layer 1 attacks are physical: wiretaps, jamming, cut cables.
